the synonymous codon usage in prokaryotic genes is strongly correlated with the intrinsic flexibility of the corresponding DNA sequence, and that this correlation is likely the result of natural selection.

the evolution of synonymous codons, which are the most abundant and highly conserved genetic elements in nature.
the functional consequences of synonymous codon choice, and how this might have influenced the early evolution of the genetic code.

the evolution of synonymous sites may have been driven by a combination of functional constraints on DNA dynamics and mRNA stability.

the DNA backbone is a dynamic structure with a complex relationship to the genetic code, and that this dynamic structure may have evolved to serve a functional purpose in addition to protein translation.
synonymous sites have been subject to a dual evolutionary pressure, with a primary function in protein coding, and an auxiliary function in optimizing the DNA backbone dynamics of the nucleoid.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the DNA backbone dynamics of the nucleoid may be subject to functional constraint, and that this constraint may have a profound effect on the evolutionary dynamics of synonymous and non synonymous sites.
codon usage is not simply a by-product of translation efficiency, but rather a consequence of a dual function for synonymous codon choice.
the genetic code may be more than just a means to specify amino acid sequences, and that codons may have evolved to encode for both protein sequences and DNA backbone dynamics.
